## The root cause

Drill-downs were tracing on whatever string they found first — and "Fulfillment Vault" came up before any real identifier. A room is a *place*, not a *thing*. Tracing it finds nothing, so you got a wall of "not recorded" and "Nothing traced".

Three fixes, all sitewide:

1. Trace order corrected. Package tag → harvest name → source harvest → manifest → production batch. Rooms, vaults and locations are now on a blocklist and can never be used as a trace term — Fulfillment Vault, Cure Vault, Freezer/Biomass Storage, Pre-Trim, Biomass Prep, Dry Rooms, Packaging, Quarantine, Solventless, Hydrocarbon, Finish Vault.

2. Stock Detail is package-level now, not aggregated. That was the deeper problem — you were clicking a *summary* row that had no identifier at all. It's now 707 individual packages, each with its Metrc tag, so every row traces. Plus a Traceability column stating in plain words whether it's traceable, and if not, why.

3. An empty trace explains itself. Instead of "No linked records found", you now get the three possible reasons, named:
- Bought in — no harvest of ours behind it; the cultivation history sits with the supplier, and the Supplier and Inbound manifest columns name who to ask
- No source recorded in Metrc — a real lineage gap to correct
- Weights never entered — the harvest exists but wet, waste and grade weights were never recorded

And if you click a room, it says plainly: "Fulfillment Vault is a place, not a product — a room cannot have a seed-to-sale history. Open an individual package from Stock Detail and trace that instead."

Filter chips fixed — no more dark text on dark. Active chips carry their state colour, inactive stay readable.

Here is the reasoning behind each call, including the ones where I chose *not* to act.

## The rule I applied throughout

A number that judges people has to be defensible to the person being judged. So every figure falls into one of three buckets, and I kept them visibly separate rather than blending them into something that merely looks authoritative:

1. Measured from your own data — strongest. Your reality beats any external benchmark.
2. Sourced from published guidance — acceptable where physics or biology doesn't care whose facility it is.
3. Nobody's number — must stay visibly flagged, never dressed up as either of the above.

The 130 g/plant mistake earlier was me putting a bucket-3 number in a bucket-1 costume. Everything since has been structured to make that impossible.

## Where I used your data over any standard

Laboratory limit → 3 days. I had an industry-ish option (14 days) and your actual distribution. Your data won: 97% of 1,938 packages inside 3 days, 95th percentile at 2. A 14-day threshold was flagging 16 packages out of 1,938 — a control that fires 0.8% of the time isn't a control, it's decoration. Set at 3, it catches genuine outliers and stays quiet otherwise.

I used the 95th percentile, not the average. An average of 0.54 days would give a threshold of ~1 day and flood you with false alarms from ordinary variation. A threshold should sit at the edge of normal, not at its centre.

Concentrate by sub-type. One flat concentrate rate was valuing rosin identically to crude. Your Inventory Value Sheet already distinguished them — $15/g solventless, $12/g live badder, $9/g cured badder — so I matched on product name and used yours. Where your sheet had no line (crude, distillate, isolate — 149 lb, the largest bucket), I fell back to the calculator's own crude cost rather than stretching a badder rate to cover it.

## Where I used published guidance

Moisture loss 70–82% → 75–80%. My original band was wider than the evidence supports, and a too-wide band means nothing ever looks abnormal. The published figure is consistent and physical — fresh cannabis is ~80% water regardless of who grew it. Tightening it moved the open-harvest figure from 702.4 lb to 625.5 lb, which is the point: the rule flows through to real numbers.

Dry window 10–14 days confirmed. My defaults happened to match the sources. I still re-sourced them rather than assume I'd been right.

Fresh frozen 4.5 kept — but note *why*: it isn't an independent number. It follows arithmetically from the moisture figures (20–25% remaining = 4:1 to 5:1). Two rules agreeing because one derives from the other is not two pieces of evidence.

## Where I deliberately refused to set a number

Harvest open limit — kept at 21 days. This is the decision I'd most want you to scrutinise. Your actual average is 65.2 days. Setting the limit to match reality would have made 26 overdue harvests vanish overnight and the register would have looked clean. That's how a metric gets quietly neutered. I left it at 21 and labelled it *"owner decision needed — kept at 21 to keep the gap visible."* If you want it changed, change it knowingly.

Ageing threshold 180 days — left flagged. No industry standard exists, and it genuinely differs by product; a vape and a pound of flower don't age alike. Inventing one would have been the 130 g/plant error again.

F2 and F4 square footage — computed but not written. F1 and F3 run 6.00 sqft/plant, so 210 plants ≈ 1,260 sqft. I put that in the input box as greyed placeholder text and nowhere else. An inference from two rooms would have become the number your room managers are judged on, and within a week nobody would remember it was a guess.

Flower at $1,100. Your own worksheets contained $741 and $1,200 in different tabs. I refused to pick, showed you the 62% spread and the ~$757,000 it swung, and you decided. Then I recorded *that it was your decision*, with a note saying it supersedes the other two — so the next person who finds $741 in the spreadsheet knows why it isn't being used.

## Structural choices

Corrections at the reporting layer, not in `v_harvest_forensic`. I'd already destroyed `mv_department_dashboard` twice with `drop … cascade`. Fixing the fresh-frozen false alarm at source would have meant rewriting a view that a great deal depends on. I wrapped it instead. Slightly less elegant, considerably less likely to blank your dashboards a third time.

Auto-detecting the package tag column instead of asking you. You'd been asked once already. Metrc tags are a fixed 24-character format starting `1A4` — the platform can test every column against that *and* against real package labels and pick the winner with a stated confidence. A question that a computer can answer shouldn't be on your list.

Overhead as one $285,000 line rather than 20 invented ones. I could have split it plausibly across electric, water, rent and insurance. Every one of those splits would have been fiction, and fiction that would later drive "which cost line is hurting us" decisions. One honest lump that says *"the total is right but nothing can be attributed to a cause"* is worth more than a detailed lie. It's structured so QuickBooks or a P&L upload replaces it cleanly.

And the one I flagged rather than assumed: whether that $285,000 includes payroll. I added it on top, because that's the normal meaning of overhead — but said plainly that if it already includes wages, the answer is $591/lb rather than $792.40. A 25% swing in your cost base shouldn't rest on my reading of one word.

So yes, it's possible — you're already doing it. 98 days from planting to first package sits inside the 105–135 day clone-to-sale window. The timeline you were given is real and your facility is capable of it.

## The one thing that stands out, and it's important

You are flowering for 51.9 days against an industry range of 56–70 — and against your own calendar, which plans 56.

That is not a rounding difference. You are pulling roughly 4 days early on average, and in the worst cases 16 days early (minimum recorded: 40 days).

Set that beside the other finding: you plan 70.1 g/sqft and deliver 34–44. Those two facts are very likely the same fact. The last two weeks of flower is when bud density and weight accumulate fastest. Harvesting at 52 days instead of 56–70 is one of the most direct ways to halve a yield — and your conversion rate is *normal* at 21.6%, which rules out drying as the cause. The weight isn't being lost after the cut. It was never grown.

Also worth noting: curing does not appear anywhere in your data. The standard allows 14–28 days of cure. Your 21.9 days cut-to-first-package covers drying and trimming only. Either you aren't curing, or it's happening inside the packaging window — which would explain part of that 84-day tail.

## What I'd check before acting

I can measure days, not trichomes. Before anyone changes the pull schedule, confirm with your grower why harvests are coming off at 52 days — if cultivars are genuinely finishing early, that's fine and the 70 g/sqft plan is simply wrong. If they're being pulled to hit the 14-day pull cadence regardless of ripeness, then the schedule is costing you roughly half your yield, and that is worth far more than every cost saving discussed today.

Your 56-day room cycle assumes 56 days of flower. You're getting 52. The calendar and the plants disagree.

Claude · 2026-08-06 12:43
You've found two genuine faults, and one of them is bad.

Vapes and edibles are counted in "each", not grams — and the platform is dividing units by 453.592 as though they were grams.

| Stream | Metrc unit | Real quantity | Shown as |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vape | each | 4,531 cartridges | "10 lb" |
| Infused (edible) | each | 17,001 units | "37.6 lb" |
| Concentrate | grams | 93,050 g | 205.2 lb ✓ |
| Dried flower | grams | 463,572 g | 1,022.3 lb ✓ |
| Pre-rolls | grams | 42,942 g | 94.6 lb ✓ |

"10 lb of vape" is meaningless — it's 4,531 cartridges. Same for edibles: not 37.6 lb, but 17,001 units. Dividing a unit count by a grams-to-pounds constant produces a number with no physical meaning, and it's been feeding valuations and dashboards.

Second fault, smaller but nastier: 2 packages of shake and trim are recorded in Metrc as `lb`, quantity 18 — and the platform divided those 18 pounds by 453.592 and displayed 0.0 lb. Eighteen pounds vanished from the totals entirely because the code assumed every quantity was grams.

On concentrates specifically — you're right to question it. They *are* recorded in grams so the pound conversion is arithmetically valid, but pounds is the wrong way to *show* them. Nobody sells or discusses badder by the pound; it's grams. Showing 205.2 lb hides that it's 93,050 g, and it's why the per-gram sub-type rates we set (rosin $15/g, live badder $12/g) look disconnected from the tile above them.

What needs doing: every stream should display in its own natural unit — flower and trim in pounds, concentrate in grams, vapes and edibles in units — with pounds shown only where it's genuinely a weight, and a dry-equivalent conversion only where one is meaningful. The fix is in `v_stock_on_hand`, which converts blindly rather than switching on `UnitOfMeasureName`.

I'm out of working context to make that change safely — it feeds the stock tiles, the flow strip, the money position and the dashboards, and a careless edit there is exactly how I blanked your dashboards twice today. It's the first thing next session, ahead of the moisture band, because the 18 lb disappearing means the totals are wrong right now, not just mislabelled.

Three things changed in the data layer, not just the display:

1. `f_to_pounds(qty, uom)` — converts grams, kilograms, milligrams, ounces and pounds correctly, and returns null for anything countable. A pound of "each" isn't a quantity of anything, so it now refuses to invent one.
2. 18.2 lb recovered. Those two packages were being divided by 453.592 and rounding to zero. They were simply absent from every total.
3. 47.5 phantom pounds removed. That was 21,532 countable units masquerading as weight in your inventory totals and, through the valuation rates, in your dollar figures.

The view keeps its original columns in their original order — so the flow strip, money position, dashboards and drill-downs don't break — with `units`, `unit_of_measure`, `sold_by_weight` and `quantity_shown` appended. `quantity_shown` gives each stream its correct phrasing: *"1,022.0 lb"* or *"4,531 Each"*.

Cultivation → Weight Audit (`v_weight_audit`) is live and permanent — it lists every unit of measure in the system, whether it's a weight, the correct pounds, what a naive grams conversion would have produced, and the error between them. If Metrc ever starts sending kilograms or ounces, it shows up there rather than silently corrupting a total.
